paragraphs: A vision model that recognizes images well may still need help turning visual observations into effective actions. This paper examines that adaptation problem for pretrained Vision Transformers. Their relatively weak built-in assumptions support large-scale pretraining, but the authors argue that missing assumptions about spatial structure may make adaptation to visual control harder.

The proposed Convolution Injector, or CoIn, adds convolutions to a pretrained transformer. Convolutions provide spatial locality: they emphasize relationships among nearby image features. They also provide translation equivariance, meaning that shifting an input produces a corresponding shift in its features. CoIn brings these control-relevant properties into the adaptation process while using the pretrained visual model.

The evaluation covers CLIP, MVP, and VC-1 across 12 control tasks in Adroit, MetaWorld, and DMC. CoIn improves performance in every tested environment and model combination. These results support the value of adding control-oriented spatial assumptions when adapting pretrained transformers, with the reported consistency applying to the combinations evaluated in the study.
icml-2024-adapting-pretrained-vits-with-.tldr: CoIn adds convolutional spatial biases to pretrained Vision Transformers and improves performance across all tested visual control settings.

paragraphs: Deep multi-view clustering groups examples using several sources of information about them. Its usefulness depends on how those views agree and how they contribute complementary information. This paper investigates whether an attacker can exploit those relationships to make the resulting groups wrong, addressing a threat that the authors describe as previously unexplored.

The attack uses a generative adversarial network to alter consistency and complementarity across views as strongly as possible. That objective gives the attacker a concrete way to target clustering without relying on an ordinary supervised prediction objective. The defense then uses adversarial training and an Attack Mitigator developed through information-theoretic analysis to support robustness.

Experiments on multi-view datasets show that the attack reduces the target model's clustering performance and that the proposed defense effectively counters such attacks. The contribution connects a clearly defined attack objective with a corresponding defense: relationships that help combine multiple views can also become attack targets, so robustness must account for how those views interact.
icml-2024-adversarially-robust-deep-mult.tldr: The paper attacks relationships among data views to disrupt clustering and develops an adversarially trained defense.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a training pattern in which a network fits its training examples well before it begins to generalize. This paper shows that the phenomenon extends beyond tightly controlled settings, including a convolutional network trained on CIFAR10 and a ResNet trained on Imagenette. It also introduces delayed robustness: resistance to adversarial examples can emerge substantially later than training fit or ordinary generalization.

The authors explain these delays through the local complexity of the network's input-output mapping. Their measure counts the density of linear regions that partition the input space. This gives a way to track how the shape of the learned function changes during training, even after training error is already very small.

For classification, the paper presents evidence of a phase transition after which these regions move away from training examples and toward decision boundaries. The mapping consequently becomes smoother around training points and less smooth near those boundaries. This changing geometry provides the proposed explanation for delayed generalization and robustness across the investigated settings.
icml-2024-deep-networks-always-grok-and-.tldr: The paper links delayed generalization and robustness to changes in network geometry and demonstrates grokking in practical image-classification settings.

paragraphs: Masked video autoencoders learn video representations by predicting missing portions of their inputs. Random masking can make them spend substantial computation and memory on patches or frames that provide little useful information. EVEREST starts from the observation that information is distributed unevenly across a video, so treating every region alike can waste resources.

The method identifies tokens rich in motion information and removes uninformative tokens during both pretraining and fine-tuning. It also introduces a frame-selection strategy designed to concentrate on informative, causal frames with little redundancy. Together, these choices focus processing on selected spatial and temporal content instead of relying only on random masking.

The authors report reduced computation and memory requirements sufficient to run pretraining and fine-tuning on one machine with eight GPUs. Performance remains comparable to resource-intensive baselines across multiple benchmarks and the uncurated Ego4D dataset. The findings suggest that more selective use of video content can preserve useful representations while reducing the hardware burden of learning them.
icml-2024-everest-efficient-masked-video.tldr: EVEREST removes uninformative video tokens and frames to reduce training costs while maintaining comparable performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning distributes optimization across participants, while adaptive gradient methods adjust learning rates during training. Combining these ideas is attractive, but existing adaptive decentralized algorithms can require many samples. This paper proposes two algorithms intended to reduce that cost for nonconvex objectives, where the optimization landscape need not have a single simple minimum.

AdaMDOS handles stochastic optimization, and AdaMDOF handles objectives formed from a finite collection of samples. The authors develop a convergence-analysis framework for both. They prove near-optimal sample complexity of approximately epsilon to the power minus three, up to logarithmic factors, for AdaMDOS. For AdaMDOF, the bound is proportional to the square root of the sample count times epsilon to the power minus two.

These guarantees concern reaching an epsilon-stationary solution, where the gradient is sufficiently small; they do not assert finding a global optimum. The authors identify AdaMDOF as the first adaptive decentralized method for the nonconvex finite-sum setting, to their knowledge. Reported experiments also demonstrate the algorithms' efficiency.
icml-2024-faster-adaptive-decentralized-.tldr: AdaMDOS and AdaMDOF provide near-optimal sample-complexity guarantees for adaptive decentralized nonconvex optimization.

paragraphs: Sampling algorithms aim to generate draws from a target probability distribution. Stochastic gradients can make this task more scalable, but their use in proximal samplers has received less attention than in Langevin methods. This paper develops a stochastic proximal sampling framework for distributions that need not be log-concave.

The convergence guarantee is conditional: the algorithm's trajectory must have a bounded second moment, and its restricted Gaussian sampling oracles must be approximated accurately enough. The authors then construct two implementable versions, SPS-SGLD and SPS-MALA, using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics and the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm, respectively.

For total-variation error epsilon in dimension d, the reported gradient complexities are approximately d times epsilon to the power minus two and square root of d times epsilon to the power minus two, suppressing logarithmic factors. The authors report an improvement of at least a dimension-to-the-one-third factor over the best-known result, again up to logarithmic terms. Synthetic-data experiments across dimensions support the proposed methods' efficiency.
icml-2024-faster-sampling-via-stochastic.tldr: Stochastic proximal samplers offer improved gradient-complexity bounds under stated moment and oracle-approximation conditions.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning dynamics model predicts how an environment changes after an action. Causal dynamics models make those predictions using relationships among entities, but the relevant relationships can depend on the current situation. This paper addresses the loss of detail that occurs when a model overlooks these context-dependent connections.

The proposed model jointly learns its predictions and a discrete latent variable that partitions the state-action space into subgroups. Each subgroup represents a context in which a relatively sparse set of dependencies can be learned. The model therefore uses different fine-grained causal structures for different parts of the space, learning those structures throughout training.

Experiments show robustness to previously unseen states and locally spurious correlations in downstream tasks that require fine-grained causal reasoning. The authors also report more effective discovery of these relationships than prior methods. The result supports learning context and dynamics together: identifying which situation applies helps determine which dependencies should guide prediction, rather than treating causal connections as equally relevant everywhere.
icml-2024-fine-grained-causal-dynamics-l.tldr: The method learns context-specific causal dynamics by quantizing state-action space, improving robustness in the evaluated reinforcement-learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies a one-layer self-attention model through prompts and the outputs sampled from it. Under suitable conditions, the authors connect its output generation to a context-conditioned Markov chain. The chain's transition matrix is reweighted using sufficient statistics of the prompt, making the role of the current context mathematically explicit.

That connection supports an analysis of when the underlying model can be learned from data. In a teacher-student setting, the authors establish identifiability and coverage conditions that guarantee consistent estimation. They also give sample-complexity guarantees for independent, identically distributed data. These results link successful recovery to what the observed prompts and outputs reveal about the model.

The paper separately examines learning from a single generated trajectory. It characterizes a winner-takes-all process in which a small set of tokens comes to dominate the context and subsequent sampling. This supplies a mathematical account of repetitive generation within the studied setting and a proposed explanation for the repetition observed in modern language models.
icml-2024-from-self-attention-to-markov-.tldr: A conditional Markov-chain formulation explains learnability and repetitive generation in a studied one-layer self-attention model.

paragraphs: Training large 3D generative models is difficult partly because detailed shapes can be expensive to represent and process. Make-A-Shape addresses this representation problem alongside the generation model itself. It is trained on 10 million publicly available shapes, making efficient handling of detailed geometry central to the approach.

The method introduces a wavelet-tree representation for high-resolution signed-distance-field shapes. A new filtering scheme retains the representation with minimal loss, while a coefficient-packing scheme makes it suitable for diffusion-based generation. A subband-adaptive training strategy further supports learning at this dataset scale. These components connect compact shape encoding with the requirements of the generative training process.

The resulting framework accepts images, point clouds, and voxels as conditioning inputs, supporting shape completion and conditional generation as well as unconditional generation. The authors report higher-quality results than existing baselines and generation within two seconds for most conditions. The findings emphasize that representation and training design can work together to enable large-scale, versatile 3D generation.
icml-2024-make-a-shape-a-ten-million-sca.tldr: Make-A-Shape combines efficient wavelet-based geometry encoding with diffusion to learn 3D generation from 10 million shapes.

paragraphs: A mechanism can encourage truthful behavior in one interaction yet lose that property when an algorithm learns which mechanism to use over time. Participants who return across rounds may act strategically to influence future choices. This paper studies how to learn mechanisms without knowing participants' type distributions while preserving incentives in the repeated setting.

At each round, the method randomly chooses between two options: the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learner, such as Hedge, and a commitment mechanism that penalizes untruthful behavior. The construction combines learning toward an application-specific objective with a direct incentive component, accounting for participants who care about later rounds.

The authors establish incentive compatibility and regret of order T raised to (1+h)/2 in an adversarial setting, where T is the number of rounds and h measures participants' long-sightedness. The dependence on h explicitly connects strategic patience to the learning guarantee. The approach applies beyond auctions, and the authors report favorable scaling with the size of the mechanism class.
icml-2024-nash-incentive-compatible-onli.tldr: Randomizing between private online learning and a truthfulness-enforcing mechanism yields incentive-compatible learning with a regret bound tied to agents' foresight.

paragraphs: Experimental design asks how to choose measurements or interventions that help learn about a system. In dynamical systems, the order of observations matters, so the data cannot generally be treated as interchangeable. This paper develops a Bayesian design method for that non-exchangeable setting by expressing design as risk-sensitive policy optimization.

The proposed Inside-Out SMC² algorithm uses nested sequential Monte Carlo to infer optimal designs. The authors then place this algorithm inside a particle Markov chain Monte Carlo framework and use gradients to amortize the policy. Here, amortization means learning a policy for making design choices, connecting the sampling-based inference procedure to a reusable decision rule.

A distinguishing feature is that the approach does not depend on contrastive estimators, which separates its construction from other amortized design techniques discussed by the authors. Numerical evaluations on a collection of dynamical systems demonstrate effectiveness relative to other state-of-the-art strategies. The contribution brings sequential data, nested particle inference, and learned design policies into one experimental-design framework.
icml-2024-nesting-particle-filters-for-e.tldr: Inside-Out SMC² combines nested particle inference and policy learning for Bayesian experimental design in dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Causal inference from observational data requires conditions that make a causal effect recoverable from what was observed. A common requirement is positivity, or overlap: relevant treatment possibilities must have positive probability. The paper examines settings where strict positivity fails and where the usual assumption of no unmeasured confounding may also fail.

The authors investigate graphical conditions that permit a particular identification formula to be used without requiring strict positivity of the entire observed distribution. They study the question through several routes: checking formulas afterward, applying do-calculus, using Q-decomposition, and taking an algorithmic approach. Relating these routes provides a unified view of how positivity requirements arise.

The paper also discusses a positivity-aware identification algorithm grounded in its theoretical characterization of formulas. The central value is a more targeted treatment of overlap: the relevant requirement is tied to the causal graph and identification formula under consideration. This supplies a framework for determining when a formula remains justified despite the failure of the conventional stronger condition.
icml-2024-on-positivity-condition-for-ca.tldr: The paper develops graphical, formula-specific positivity conditions for causal identification without strict positivity of the full observed distribution.

paragraphs: Deep regression models predict numerical values, making failure detection a question of identifying potentially unreliable predictions. Existing approaches often use uncertainty about the model or measure how inconsistent an example is with the training data. This paper finds that uncertainty is necessary but insufficient to characterize failures accurately in practice.

The authors introduce PAGER, a framework for systematically detecting and describing failures in deep regressors. It builds on anchored training and combines epistemic uncertainty with complementary manifold non-conformity scores. These scores add a view of how an example relates to the structure of the data, supplementing the model's uncertainty estimate rather than treating that estimate as a complete account.

PAGER uses the combined signals to organize samples into distinct risk regimes. This makes failure characterization more informative than relying on uncertainty alone: different examples can be assessed through both model uncertainty and non-conformity. The stated contribution is a unified framework for distinguishing these risk patterns, motivated by proactive detection before unreliable regression outputs lead to costly errors.
icml-2024-pager-accurate-failure-charact.tldr: PAGER combines model uncertainty and manifold non-conformity to characterize failure risks in deep regression.

paragraphs: Bayesian experimental design chooses experiments to improve knowledge of unknown parameters. PASOA tackles two linked tasks: selecting the next design and accurately updating the posterior distribution after each step. It combines a contrastive estimation principle, stochastic optimization, and sequential Monte Carlo sampling to maximize expected information gain.

The difficulty is that informative experiments can move successive posterior distributions far apart. That movement can undermine ordinary sequential Monte Carlo, even though obtaining information is the design objective. PASOA uses tempering to handle the transition between distributions, aiming to preserve sampling accuracy while still selecting experiments with large information gains. The authors show that this component is crucial to performance.

The resulting procedure treats design optimization and parameter inference jointly, rather than assuming the posterior estimates will remain accurate automatically. The paper proves a consistency property for its optimal-design estimators. Numerical experiments demonstrate the approach's potential and report better performance than other recent procedures, supporting the combination of tempered sampling with stochastic design optimization.
icml-2024-pasoa-particle-based-bayesian-.tldr: PASOA combines stochastic design optimization with tempered particle sampling to seek informative experiments while maintaining accurate posterior estimates.

paragraphs: Foundation models have gained broad capabilities through training on internet-scale data, but continually self-improving, open-ended AI remains elusive. This position paper argues that the ingredients for open-endedness are now available. It further claims that open-endedness is an essential property of artificial superhuman intelligence, presenting this as a research position rather than an achieved system.

The authors give a formal definition built around novelty and learnability, evaluated with respect to a human observer. Those two ideas connect the production of something new with the observer's ability to learn from it. The paper then outlines a route toward superhuman intelligence through foundation-model-based systems capable of making novel discoveries relevant to people.

The final part examines safety implications of generally capable open-ended systems. Its significance lies in linking a proposed definition, a development direction, and a safety agenda around the same property. The authors expect open-ended foundation models to become an increasingly productive and safety-critical research area; that expectation remains part of their forward-looking argument.
icml-2024-position-open-endedness-is-ess.tldr: This position paper argues that human-relevant open-ended discovery is essential to superhuman AI and could be built on foundation models.

paragraphs: Different neural networks can organize information in increasingly similar ways despite differences in their training or inputs. This position paper argues that such representational convergence is a broad trend. It surveys examples from the literature across domains and over time, focusing on how models' internal representations become more aligned.

The authors also demonstrate convergence between vision and language models: as the models become larger, their assessments of distances between data points become more alike. This comparison concerns the relationships models assign among examples. It provides evidence that models working with different kinds of data can develop increasingly similar representational organization.

The larger hypothesis is that these trends point toward a shared statistical representation of reality, which the authors call a platonic representation. They discuss possible pressures that could favor convergence, along with implications, limitations, and counterexamples. The observed alignment and the proposed destination remain distinct claims: the paper presents evidence of convergence while treating a common model of reality as a hypothesis.
icml-2024-position-the-platonic-represen.tldr: The paper argues that model representations are converging and hypothesizes a shared statistical representation of reality.

paragraphs: Molecular docking predicts how a ligand binds to a protein, an important problem in drug design. Existing learning-based approaches can depend on an already-bound protein structure or overlook the conformations of sidechains in the binding pocket. These choices restrict practical usefulness and can produce unrealistic predictions of the binding arrangement.

Re-Dock addresses flexible docking, where the ligand pose and pocket-sidechain poses are predicted together. It uses a diffusion bridge generative model extended to geometric manifolds, allowing the generation process to account for the geometry of these conformations. An energy-to-geometry mapping inspired by the Newton-Euler equation connects binding energy with the predicted structures.

The joint treatment matters because the task concerns both where the ligand sits and how the surrounding pocket is configured. The authors evaluate Re-Dock on designed benchmarks including apo-dock and cross-dock and report better effectiveness and efficiency than current methods. These findings support an energy-constrained generative approach to docking that explicitly includes flexibility in the binding pocket.
icml-2024-re-dock-towards-flexible-and-r.tldr: Re-Dock jointly predicts ligand and pocket-sidechain poses using a geometric diffusion bridge tied to binding energy.

paragraphs: Vector quantization compresses vectors by representing them with entries from codebooks. Residual quantization does this in stages: each stage approximates the error left by earlier choices. Conventional residual quantization uses a fixed codebook at each stage, even though the remaining error depends on which codewords were selected before it.

QINCo replaces those fixed stage-specific codebooks with specialized codebooks constructed by a neural model. Each codebook depends on the current approximation assembled from previous stages. This makes the next quantization step responsive to the particular error it needs to encode, directly addressing the dependency ignored by the conventional approach.

Experiments show substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods across several datasets and code sizes. On BigANN1M and Deep1M, QINCo achieves better nearest-neighbor search accuracy with 12-byte codes than UNQ achieves with 16-byte codes. That comparison illustrates the practical significance of conditioning codebooks on earlier choices: in these evaluations, more accurate search is possible with a smaller stored representation per vector.
icml-2024-residual-quantization-with-imp.tldr: QINCo adapts residual-quantization codebooks to earlier encoding choices, improving search accuracy with compact vector codes.

paragraphs: Transformers have strong results in language and vision, yet simpler linear models can outperform them in long-term forecasting of multiple time series. This paper investigates that gap through a toy linear forecasting problem. In that setting, the authors show that transformers fail to converge to the true solution despite having enough expressive power.

The analysis identifies attention as responsible for the poor generalization in the studied problem. Building on that finding, the authors propose SAMformer, a shallow, lightweight transformer using channel-wise attention and sharpness-aware optimization. They report that this optimization approach allows the model to escape bad local minima, connecting forecasting performance to how the model is trained.

Experiments extend the findings to commonly used real-world multivariate time-series datasets. SAMformer surpasses the compared state-of-the-art methods and matches the largest MOIRAI foundation model while using substantially fewer parameters. The results support the paper's emphasis on attention and optimization: a compact transformer can perform strongly when its training avoids the failure behavior identified in the analysis.
icml-2024-samformer-unlocking-the-potent.tldr: SAMformer combines a lightweight transformer with sharpness-aware optimization to improve multivariate long-term forecasting.

paragraphs: Monotonicity constraints encode an expected direction of change between inputs and outputs. They can help make scientific models more plausible and support fairness in automated decisions. Min-max neural networks guarantee monotonicity, but their minimum and maximum operations can produce zero derivatives that leave training stuck in undesirable local optima.

The paper replaces those extrema operations with smooth minimum and maximum functions that are strictly increasing. The resulting smooth min-max module alleviates the training problem while retaining the original architecture's asymptotic approximation properties. It can also be included in larger deep-learning systems and trained together with their other components.

The authors describe the module as conceptually simple and computationally cheaper than state-of-the-art neural approaches to monotonic modeling. Their experiments find that this reduced computational burden does not sacrifice generalization compared with the evaluated neural and non-neural alternatives. The contribution is therefore both architectural and practical: smoothing the operations improves trainability while preserving the useful function-approximation properties of the monotonic construction.
icml-2024-smooth-min-max-monotonic-netwo.tldr: Smooth min-max networks improve the trainability of monotonic models while retaining approximation properties and competitive generalization.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior by choosing a distribution from a manageable family. This paper studies mixtures of Gaussians with fixed covariance, extending theoretical analysis beyond a single Gaussian approximation. Holding covariance fixed focuses the optimization on where the Gaussian components are located.

The authors express the mixture as point masses smoothed by a Gaussian kernel. Its discrepancy from the target is measured by a mollified relative entropy, a Kullback-Leibler divergence involving that smoothed distribution. Optimizing the mixture then becomes a problem of moving particles representing component locations. Gradient descent on those positions takes the form of an interacting particle system.

The analysis separates optimization error from approximation error. A descent lemma establishes that each algorithm iteration decreases the objective. A second result upper-bounds the discrepancy between an optimal finite mixture and the target distribution. These address different questions: whether the algorithm makes progress and how closely the chosen mixture family can represent the target. Neither statement alone amounts to exact recovery of an arbitrary posterior.
icml-2024-theoretical-guarantees-for-var.tldr: The paper gives objective-descent and approximation-error guarantees for variational inference with fixed-covariance Gaussian mixtures.

paragraphs: Understanding molecular geometry requires relationships that involve more than isolated pairs of atoms. The paper argues that graph transformers typically lack third-order interactions, limiting their geometric understanding. Its Triplet Graph Transformer, or TGT, adds direct communication between pairs belonging to a shared group of three nodes.

Novel triplet-attention and aggregation mechanisms implement this communication. For molecular property prediction, TGT first predicts distances between atoms from a two-dimensional molecular graph, then uses those distances in downstream tasks. A three-stage training procedure and stochastic inference further improve training efficiency and model performance, supporting the use of predicted geometry within the overall workflow.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on PCQM4Mv2 and OC20 IS2RE, plus transfer-learning results on QM9, MOLPCBA, and LIT-PCBA. They also demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the traveling salesman problem. Together, these evaluations support the usefulness of triplet interactions for molecular learning and show that the architecture's reported benefits extend to an additional graph-based problem beyond molecular property prediction.
icml-2024-triplet-interaction-improves-g.tldr: TGT adds interactions among node triplets to improve molecular geometry and property learning, with strong results on several benchmarks.

paragraphs: Training language models with human preferences can change their behavior, but understanding how those changes unfold remains a theoretical challenge. This paper offers an initial analysis of alignment learning dynamics. It focuses on how the distribution of examples in a preference dataset affects the model's updates during training.

The authors formally connect that data distribution to the rate of model updates and establish guarantees on training accuracy. Their theory also identifies a tendency for optimization to favor behaviors whose preferences are more distinguishable. This means the ease of distinguishing preferred behavior can influence what training prioritizes, making the composition of preference data relevant to the learning process itself.

Experiments on contemporary language models and alignment tasks support the theoretical findings. The contribution links empirical alignment behavior to a mathematical account of update rates and uneven prioritization. Its accuracy guarantees concern training, while the broader insight is that different behaviors can receive different emphasis during optimization because of how clearly their preferences are expressed in the data.
icml-2024-understanding-the-learning-dyn.tldr: The paper shows how preference-data distributions shape alignment updates and can favor behaviors with more distinguishable preferences.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization is often considered poorly suited to problems with many input dimensions. Many proposed remedies simplify the objective by assuming it has a particular structure. This paper investigates why standard Bayesian optimization deteriorates in high dimensions and interprets both that failure and existing remedies through model complexity.

The proposed change is simple: scale the prior over the Gaussian process lengthscale with the number of dimensions. Lengthscales control how the model relates function values at different inputs. Adjusting their prior changes the model's assumed complexity, bringing it to a manageable level without imposing structural restrictions on the objective being optimized.

The authors report substantial improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple commonly studied real-world high-dimensional tasks. These results suggest that standard Bayesian optimization can perform much better in such settings when its prior is adjusted appropriately. The central lesson concerns the modeling assumptions: dimension-dependent prior design can address important failure behavior without requiring a more elaborate optimization framework or restrictive objective structure.
icml-2024-vanilla-bayesian-optimization-.tldr: Scaling the Gaussian process lengthscale prior with dimension substantially improves standard Bayesian optimization on evaluated high-dimensional tasks.

paragraphs: An agent transferring between related tasks needs a useful description of what has changed. This paper addresses that representation problem in reinforcement learning, where tasks can differ in rewards or transition dynamics. The goal is transfer at run time without additional training, using a representation that relates the current task to previously encountered ones.

The proposed function encoder expresses a function as a weighted combination of learned nonlinear basis functions. Applied to a reward function or transition function, the resulting weights provide a coherent vector description of the task. That common representation gives the agent information about relationships among tasks, supporting reuse of what it has already learned.

The authors augment basic reinforcement-learning algorithms with these function-encoder task representations. Across three reinforcement-learning fields, they report state-of-the-art data efficiency, asymptotic performance, and training stability. The contribution centers on representing task-defining functions: encoding rewards or dynamics in a shared learned basis enables the reported zero-shot transfer between related tasks without further training at run time.
icml-2024-zero-shot-reinforcement-learni.tldr: Function encoders represent rewards or dynamics in a learned basis to enable transfer between related reinforcement-learning tasks without additional training.
